```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>"
)
library(daos)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

The **daos** package is a collection of utility functions built for
day-to-day statistical work. This vignette walks through every function
with short, self-contained examples.

Five bodies of work that started here have since grown into packages of
their own, and are not covered below:
[taskr](https://github.com/dataniel/taskr) for task management,
[statbank](https://github.com/dataniel/statbank) for the Greenland and
Faroese statbanks, [cvrr](https://github.com/dataniel/cvrr) for published
Danish annual reports, [taxmill](https://github.com/dataniel/taxmill)
for milling PDF financial statements into data, and
[pathr](https://github.com/dataniel/pathr) for the file browser and the
RStudio addins that take the friction out of Windows paths. None of them
depends on daos, or daos on them.

---

## Convenience shorthands

### `f()`: string interpolation

`f()` is a short alias for `glue::glue()`, inspired by Python's f-string
syntax. The name is not self-explanatory, but it is fast to type and
stays out of the way in a pipeline.

```{r}
year <- 2026
f("Report for {year}")
f("1 + 1 = {1 + 1}")
```

### `nowf()`: formatted timestamp

`nowf()` combines `format()` and `Sys.time()` in a single call, so you
can timestamp an export inline without stopping to look up the
`format(Sys.time(), ...)` signature.

```{r}
nowf()                  # default: YYYYMMDD
nowf("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")  # custom format
```

A typical use is timestamping an export file:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
iris |>
  writexl::write_xlsx(f("iris_{nowf('%Y%B')}.xlsx"))
```

### `shh()`: suppress messages and warnings

A shorthand for `suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(...))`. Useful when
you are tired of tidyverse startup banners, or when an R script runs as
a CLI tool (e.g. with `rapp`) or in a presentation tool like
`presenterm`, where console output has to be clean. The odd name is on
purpose: a function called `quiet` is one masking conflict away from
trouble.

```{r}
shh(message("this will not appear"))
shh(warning("neither will this"))
```

### `is_blank()`: comprehensive blank test

`is.na()` only catches `NA`, and `rlang::is_empty()` only catches `NULL`
and zero-length vectors. `is_blank()` covers all three plus empty
strings, which is handy when validating input that can arrive in any of
these forms.

```{r}
is_blank(NULL)        # TRUE
is_blank(NA)          # TRUE
is_blank("")          # TRUE
is_blank(c(NA, NA))   # TRUE
is_blank(0)           # FALSE
is_blank("text")      # FALSE
```

### `%??%`: null-coalescing with blank detection

Like `rlang::%||%` but uses `is_blank()` instead of `is.null()`, so it
also triggers on `NA`, `""`, and empty vectors.

```{r}
NULL %??% "default"
NA   %??% 0
""   %??% "unknown"
42   %??% 99          # returns 42
```

### `%like%`: regex matching with NA preservation

`%like%` is a more readable replacement for `str_detect()`.
The infix form reads naturally in a `filter()` call, and unlike
`grepl()`, `NA` values stay `NA` instead of being coerced to `FALSE`.
That matters when filtering on optional fields.

```{r}
c("sedan", "SUV", NA, "truck") %like% "^S"

# In a dplyr pipeline:
filter(ggplot2::mpg, model %like% "\\d+") |>
  count(model)
```

---

## File workflows

### `read_files()`: validate, read, and collect

Reading a set of files normally takes a small pipeline: `list.files()`,
a loop or `purrr::map()`, and manual naming. `read_files()` does it in
one call and handles path expansion, existence checks, format detection,
and naming along the way.

A single path returns the object directly; multiple paths return a named
list with a progress bar.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Single file (returns object directly):
df <- read_files("data/results.parquet")

# Multiple files with glue expansion:
lst <- read_files("data/dat{0:9}.parquet", names = 0:9)
```

Supported formats: `csv`, `tsv`, `parquet`, `feather`, `xlsx`, `xls`,
`rds`, `sas7bdat`, `sav`, `por`, `xpt`, `dta`, `json`, `ndjson`,
`jsonl`, `yaml`, `yml`, `txt`.

In practice, `read_files()` works best when data production is
consistent: same formats, same column names, same types across files.
If `read_files()` handles a set of files without warnings, the workflow
is in order. When it warns about type mismatches, something has changed
upstream. There is a separate article about this way of working, and
about using `view_types()` when files refuse to stack:
`vignette("read-files")`.

Supply a custom reader to override auto-detection or add arguments:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
read_files(
  "data/dat{0:9}.parquet",
  reader = \(x) arrow::read_parquet(x, col_select = 1:5)
)
```

**Column name casing**

By default, column names are converted to lowercase after reading
(`.lowercase = TRUE`). Set `.lowercase = FALSE` to preserve original
casing.

**Binding into one tibble**

Set `out = "bind"` to row-bind all files. Use `.id` to track the origin
of each row. When `names` is a numeric vector (e.g. years), the `.id`
column will also be numeric.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
read_files(
  "data/dat{2020:2024}.parquet",
  names = 2020:2024,
  out   = "bind",
  .id   = "year"
)
```

If column types differ across files, a warning is issued and types are
reconciled with `readr::type_convert()`. The `.id` column is always
excluded from this reconciliation.

**Unpacking into individual variables**

Set `out = "unpack"` to assign each file as its own named variable in
the calling environment. By default, `read_files()` aborts if any name
already exists. Set `.overwrite = TRUE` to allow overwriting.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
read_files("data/dat{0:9}.parquet", names = paste0("dat", 0:9), out = "unpack")
```

### `summon()`: retrieve objects by name pattern

A regex-based alternative to `ls()` + `mget()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mget(ls(pattern = "dat\\d"))   # base R
summon("dat\\d")               # daos
```

`summon()` pairs naturally with `out = "unpack"` to collect a family of
objects back into a list:

```{r}
dat1 <- data.frame(x = 1)
dat2 <- data.frame(x = 2)
dat3 <- data.frame(x = 3)

result <- summon("^dat\\d+$")
names(result)
```

### `read_access()`: read from a Microsoft Access database

Connects to an `.mdb` or `.accdb` file via ODBC, executes a SQL query,
and returns the result as a tibble. Requires the `DBI` and `odbc`
packages and a Microsoft Access ODBC driver.

The `verbosity` argument controls output:

- `"compact"` (default): one line per file, best when looping
- `"full"`: header, spinners, and summary, best for single files
- `"quiet"`: no output

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Full output for interactive use:
df <- read_access("data/sales.mdb", "SELECT * FROM Customers",
                  verbosity = "full")

# Loop over many databases quietly:
files <- list.files("data", pattern = "\\.mdb$", full.names = TRUE)
results <- lapply(files, \(f) read_access(f, "SELECT * FROM Sales"))
```

### `write_excel()`: write presentable Excel files

This function exists because a plain data export is hard to read
for the people the file is meant for. The complaint from a colleague who
works with macroeconomic statistics was concrete: no frozen header, no
thousand separators, no rounding. `writexl::write_xlsx()` is fast but
writes exactly such unformatted files, and `openxlsx2` can do all the
styling but wants a workbook object, worksheets, styles, and a save
call. `write_excel()` sits in between: one call, with defaults that make
the file presentable.

- Numeric columns with at least one value ≥ 1,000 are formatted with a
  thousand separator and no displayed decimals (`#,##0`); the underlying
  values are preserved. Use `digits = 2` for two displayed decimals, or
  `digits = NULL` to disable automatic numeric formatting. This applies to
  columns with an absolute value of at least 1,000.
- Year-like columns are excluded automatically: a numeric column where
  every value is a whole number between 1800 and 2200 is assumed to hold
  years, so `2020` is not displayed as `2.020`. Disable with
  `detect_years = FALSE`, and use `skip_fmt` for columns the heuristic
  cannot guess (e.g. numeric period codes like `202001`).
- `NA` values appear as blank cells.
- The header row is bold.
- The first row is frozen (can be turned off with `freeze_header = FALSE`).

Only `.xlsx` can be written. The old binary `.xls` format is not
supported, and a non-`.xlsx` path fails early instead of producing a
file Excel will complain about.

**Writing a new file**

Pass a data frame or a named list of data frames. The default `mode = "new"`
fails if the file already exists. Use `mode = "overwrite"` to replace the
entire workbook.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Single data frame: sheet name defaults to "Sheet1"
write_excel(mtcars, "output.xlsx")

# Named list: each element becomes a sheet
write_excel(
  list(Cars = mtcars, Iris = iris),
  "output.xlsx"
)
```

**Sheet naming**

Sheet names come from the list names. Unnamed elements get default names
(`"Sheet1"`, `"Sheet2"`, ...). Mixed naming is also fine:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# "Hoved" is explicit; second sheet becomes "Sheet2"
write_excel(list(Hoved = mtcars, iris), "output.xlsx")
```

**Appending sheets to an existing file**

`mode = "append"` adds sheets to an existing file and fails on name collisions.
Use `mode = "replace"` to replace matching sheets and add any new ones. Names
are matched ignoring case; replaced sheets keep their position, and other
sheets are retained. Both modes require an existing file and operate on
whole sheets, not individual rows.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
write_excel(list(Hoved = mtcars), "output.xlsx")
write_excel(list(Bilag = iris), "output.xlsx", mode = "append")
write_excel(list(Hoved = mtcars), "output.xlsx", mode = "replace")
```

**Other options**

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Insert as an Excel table (filter arrows, banded rows)
write_excel(mtcars, "output.xlsx", as_table = TRUE)

# Exclude columns from the #,##0 format
write_excel(mtcars, "output.xlsx", skip_fmt = "hp")
```

### `read_ta()` / `write_ta()`: read and write Greenlandic TA files

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df <- read_ta("ta.file")
write_ta(df, "ta.file")
```

`write_ta()` only writes what `read_ta()` reads back unchanged. Values that
would not fit their fixed-width field, or would lose decimals, stop with an
error that lists them, so no file with shifted fields is written.

### `read_ta2()` / `write_ta2()`: the new TA layout

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df <- read_ta2("ta.file")
write_ta2(df, "ta.file")
```

The new TA system uses a 140-character layout with nine columns. The `2`
functions handle it with the same guarantee as `write_ta()`; the old pair is
kept for the transition and for old files. `read_ta2()` refuses lines shorter
than 140 characters, so an old-layout file is never read into the wrong
columns.

## Data inspection

### `view_types()`: compare column types across data frames

`view_types()` is `glimpse()` across several data frames at once: one
row per column, with the type in each dataset. Useful before a join, or
before binding with `read_files(out = "bind")`.

```{r}
df_a <- data.frame(x = 1L,  y = "a", z = TRUE)
df_b <- data.frame(x = 1.0, y = "b", z = 1L)

view_types(df_a, df_b)
```

```{r}
# Only columns where types differ:
view_types(df_a, df_b, diff = TRUE)
```

The `focus` argument checks that a specific column has an expected type
and returns only the datasets where it does not:

```{r}
view_types(df_a, df_b, focus = c(x = "int"))
```

---

## Data validation

The checkpoint pattern behind these two functions has its own article,
`vignette("validation")`, which shows how to build lightweight
validation into pipelines with them.

### `expect_empty()`: assert a data frame is empty

Often you want to assert that a filter finds nothing, and to hear about
it right away when it does. Writing a custom
`if (nrow(x) > 0) cli::cli_abort(...)` every time gets repetitive.
`expect_empty()` does it in one step, fits into a pipeline, and can
write to a log file.

Filter for the rows that should not exist, pipe them in, and the
offending rows are at hand the moment something goes wrong.

```{r}
# Success:
dplyr::starwars |>
  filter(name == "Harry Potter") |>
  expect_empty(
    success_msg = "No Harry Potter rows in starwars",
    warn_msg    = "Unexpected fictional character found"
  )
```

```{r}
# Warning: rows found
dplyr::starwars |>
  filter(mass > 1000) |>
  expect_empty(warn_msg = "Unrealistic mass values")
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Hard abort:
dplyr::starwars |>
  filter(mass > 1000) |>
  expect_empty(abort_msg = "Unrealistic mass values")
```

The `log` argument writes a timestamped entry to a file, so when a
scheduled run misbehaves, the errors are already collected by the time
you sit down to investigate:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
log_path <- f("log/{nowf()}/checks.log")
checker  <- \(data, ...) expect_empty(data, ..., log = log_path)

dplyr::starwars |>
  filter(name == "Harry Potter") |>
  checker(success_msg = "No fictional characters")

dplyr::starwars |>
  filter(height > 250) |>
  checker(warn_msg = "Unusually tall characters")
```

### `flag_duplicates()`: detect and label duplicate rows

Base R's `duplicated()` only marks the second occurrence of a duplicate.
`flag_duplicates()` marks all copies and gives them a shared group ID,
so the whole group can be inspected together. The ID can also serve as
an implicit record linkage key: if several respondents have reported the
same information but background data is missing for one of them, the
shared `dupid` reveals the connection.

```{r}
flag_duplicates(ggplot2::mpg)
```

```{r}
# Check specific columns:
flag_duplicates(ggplot2::mpg, manufacturer, model, year) |>
  filter(isdup) |>
  arrange(dupid)
```

Combine with `expect_empty()` for a pipeline validation gate:

```{r}
ggplot2::mpg |>
  flag_duplicates() |>
  filter(isdup) |>
  expect_empty(warn_msg = "Duplicate rows detected")
```

## Data manipulation

### `drop_empty_rows()` and `drop_empty_cols()`: selective removal

Choose which columns determine whether a row is empty, so an ID or metadata
column does not keep an otherwise empty observation. Selection works like
`select()`: names, ranges, `starts_with()`, `where(is.numeric)`, and `all_of()`.
With no selection, every column is inspected.

```{r}
df <- tibble::tibble(
  id = 1:3,
  score_a = c(1, NA, NA),
  score_b = c(NA_real_, NA_real_, NA_real_),
  comment = c("ok", "", "  ")
)

# Inspect the score columns; keep every column in retained rows.
drop_empty_rows(df, starts_with("score_"))

# Only numeric columns are candidates for removal; id is not empty.
drop_empty_cols(df, where(is.numeric))

# Include empty and whitespace-only text, without modifying retained values.
drop_empty_rows(df, comment, blank = TRUE)

# Combine row and column removal explicitly.
df |> drop_empty_rows(starts_with("score_")) |> drop_empty_cols()
```

By default, only missing values (`NA` and `NaN`) count as empty.
`blank = TRUE` also handles blank character values and factor labels.
Zero and `FALSE` always count as data. A row is removed only when **all**
selected values are empty. Column removal only affects the selected columns.

An empty selection changes nothing. Zero-row inputs retain their column
schema; zero-column inputs retain their rows. Grouped data is assessed over
the whole input, and grouping metadata is updated when columns are removed.

### `split_by()`: split a data frame into a named list

`dplyr::group_split()` returns an unnamed list. `split_by()` adds names
derived from the grouping values, making it straightforward to index by
group:

```{r}
parts <- split_by(ggplot2::mpg, manufacturer)
names(parts)[1:5]
head(parts[["audi"]])
```

Multiple grouping columns are joined with `.sep`:

```{r}
parts2 <- split_by(ggplot2::mpg, cyl, drv, .sep = "-")
names(parts2)[1:4]
```

## Domain-specific

### `clean_cpr()` / `clean_cvr()`: standardise identifier columns

Identifiers rarely arrive in one consistent shape: `111111-1118`,
`12 34 56 78`, `DK12345678`, or a nine-digit CPR that lost its leading
zero in Excel. Before a join, both sides need the same form, and that is
all these two functions do. They take a vector and return a vector, so
the natural place for them is inside a `mutate()`:

```{r}
clean_cpr(c("111111-1118", "101004007", "1111111118"))
clean_cvr(c("DK12345678", "12 34 56 78", "12345678"))
```

The two differ on one point. `clean_cpr()` zero-pads nine-digit values,
because birth days 01 to 09 mean that a third of all CPR numbers start
with a zero, which Excel drops. `clean_cvr()` never adds a digit: a
seven-digit CVR cannot be told apart from a typo, and padding it would
let a malformed number slip past a later `cvr %like% "^\\d{8}$"`
checkpoint.

Neither function validates. Malformed values come back cleaned but still
visibly malformed. Validation is `add_cpr_info()`'s job (below), or a
checkpoint from `vignette("validation")`.

### `format_db07()`: choose the format of DB07 industry codes

DB07 industry codes appear both as `011100` and `01.11.00` depending on
the source. `format_db07()` automatically handles mixed input with dots,
whitespace, or digits only. Choose `"dotted"` (the default) or `"compact"`
output without specifying the input format. Any aggregation level works:

```{r}
format_db07(c("011100", "01.1100", "0111", "011"))
format_db07(c("011100", "01.11.00", "01 11 00"), format = "compact")
```

Like the `clean_*` functions, `format_db07()` never invents digits:
a code that lost its leading
zero in Excel is ambiguous (`111` could be group `11.1` or class `01.11`),
so keep industry codes as character columns.

### `db_label()`: add Danish industry labels

Use `db_label()` to add a label column from a DB code. Always specify
`version = "DB07"` or `version = "DB25"`; identical codes can have different
meanings in the two classifications.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(dbkode = c("011200", "01.49.10", NA))
df |> dplyr::mutate(branche_label = db_label(dbkode, version = "DB07"))
db_label(c("A", "01", "01.1", "01.11"), version = "DB25")
```

Labels come from the bundled DST tables and work offline. Input can contain
dots or whitespace. Unknown codes return `NA` with a warning; missing values
stay missing. Keep leading zeroes in character codes.

### Convert industry codes between DB07 and DB25

For mixed data, inspect the source codes before converting:

```{r}
inspect_db(c("014910", "014800", "253000", "011200", NA))
```

`db07_only` and `db25_only` indicate membership in just one classification.
`both` means the version cannot be determined from the code alone: `253000`
has different meanings in DB07 and DB25. Both labels are returned for review.
Identical labels also leave the version unresolved. Use source metadata and
the original industry text and time context to investigate these rows.
The inspection supports full six-digit codes only.

`convert_db07_to_db25()` and `convert_db25_to_db07()` use bundled keys from
[Statistics Denmark](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/dansk-branchekode-er-gaeldende)
(source page updated 26 February 2026), so no internet connection is needed.
Both accept full six-digit codes with or without dots and whitespace:

```{r}
convert_db07_to_db25(c("011100", "01.49.10", NA))
convert_db25_to_db07("25.30.00", format = "compact")
```

By default, a code with multiple possible destinations returns `NA` with
a warning. To choose DST's simplified mapping explicitly:

```{r}
convert_db07_to_db25("01.19.00", method = "simple")
convert_db25_to_db07("01.48.00", method = "simple")
```

The simplified matrices are specific to each direction and use numbers of
units, not economic activity. They are approximate and should not be used
as weights to distribute turnover. A round trip need not recover the
original code. Invalid lengths and unknown codes return `NA` with a warning;
missing values remain missing. Leading zeroes are not guessed.

### `add_cpr_info()`: add birth date, age, sex, and validity

`add_cpr_info()` appends selected information while preserving the original
CPR column. Dashes, spaces, and lost leading zeroes are handled internally.
Use `clean_cpr()` explicitly if you also want to standardise the source column.

Both functions share the same native cleaning rules. `add_cpr_info()` parses
each CPR once for all requested outputs, including multiple age calculations.
You do not need a separate cleaning step just to calculate CPR information.
Use an explicit cleaning step when the identifier will also be used for joins
or export:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
df |>
  dplyr::mutate(pnr = clean_cpr(pnr)) |>
  add_cpr_info(pnr, age(year), sex, bday)
```

`clean_cpr()` is idempotent: cleaning again gives the same values. Already
standardised character vectors are returned without a replacement vector.

Without selections, the function adds `bday`, `age`, `sex`, `mod11`, and `valid`.
Bare `age` and `age()` use today's date; explicit references make analysis
reproducible.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(
  pnr = c("1111111118", "111111-1118", "111111118"),
  year = c(2024L, 2025L, 2026L)
)
add_cpr_info(df, pnr)
add_cpr_info(df, pnr, sex, birth_date = bday)
```

Write `output_name = calculation` to rename a result. Each age calculation
has its own reference, so several ages can be added in one call:

```{r}
df |>
  add_cpr_info(
    pnr,
    primoalder = age(year),
    medioalder = age(year, "medio"),
    ultimoalder = age(year, "ultimo"),
    sex,
    bday
  )
```

`age(year)` defaults to `"primo"` with `primo = "previous_ultimo"`
(31 December of the previous year); `"medio"` means 1 July and
`"ultimo"` means 31 December. `year` can be a scalar, a column, or an
expression evaluated in the original input data.

This default makes opening ages equal to the previous year's closing ages.
It can also be written explicitly:

```{r}
add_cpr_info(df, pnr, primoalder = age(year, primo = "previous_ultimo"))
```

Someone born on 1 January 2000 is then 0 in counting year 2001;
`age(year, primo = "jan1")` instead includes that day's birthday and gives 1.

For a specific date, use `age(date = ...)` with a Date or ISO date string.
Supply one reference for all rows or one per row. Missing references give
missing ages. Use `.env$name` to explicitly access a caller variable when
a column has the same name.

```{r}
add_cpr_info(df, pnr, alder = age(date = "2025-07-01"))
df$reference <- as.Date(paste0(df$year, "-01-01"))
add_cpr_info(df, pnr, alder = age(date = reference))
```

Existing output names cause an error with guidance to rename the selection
or use `overwrite = TRUE`. Duplicate output names are always an error, and
the source CPR column cannot be overwritten.

`valid` means ten digits encoding a real calendar date, not confirmation
that the CPR number was assigned. Missing and invalid CPR values give
`valid = FALSE`. `mod11` is an independent checksum and is not part of
`valid`. Choose `mod11` explicitly when selecting outputs if you need it.

The former `add`, `ref_date`, `year`, and `at` arguments are replaced by
selections and `age()`. For example, `add = c(alder = "age"), year = year`
becomes `alder = age(year)`. The source CPR column is now preserved.

Age counts completed calendar years, not elapsed days divided by 365.25.
For a person born on 29 February, age increases on 29 February in leap
years and on 1 March in non-leap years. For a birth date of 29 February 2000:

| Reference date | Age |
| --- | ---: |
| 2024-02-28 | 23 |
| 2024-02-29 | 24 |
| 2024-03-01 | 24 |
| 2025-02-28 | 24 |
| 2025-03-01 | 25 |

`age(2024)` means age on 31 December 2023.
by default, giving age 23 in this example.

## Interactive tools

### `screen_timeseries()`: interactive time-series screening

It is hard to get as close to data in a console as in Excel, where the
feedback is immediate and visual. `screen_timeseries()` is an attempt to
bridge that gap. It launches a Shiny app where you walk through the time
series group by group, zoom, and flag anomalies -- without writing any
filtering code.

All columns that are not `x`, `y`, `series`, or excluded automatically
become dropdown filters. Requires `shiny` and `plotly`. Group row indices
are prepared once, and plots are built directly with Plotly for fast navigation.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df <- expand.grid(
  year    = 2010:2020,
  country = c("DK", "SE", "NO", "FI")
)
df$gdp <- rnorm(nrow(df), mean = 300, sd = 30)

screen_timeseries(df, x = year, y = gdp)

# Multiple lines per group with series:
ggplot2::economics_long |>
  mutate(group = "Economics") |>
  screen_timeseries(date, value, series = variable, .exclude = value01)
```

**Keyboard shortcuts**

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `<-` / `->` | Navigate to previous / next group |
| `Space` | Flag the current group |
| `R` | Reset zoom |
| `Q` | Quit and return flagged groups |

The `.y_min` and `.y_max` arguments fix the Y-axis bounds globally
across all groups. The `.title` argument sets a title shown in the app
header and in downloaded figures:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
screen_timeseries(df, year, gdp,
                  .y_min = 0, .y_max = 500,
                  .title = "GDP by country")
```

Press **Q**, click **Finish**, or close the browser session to end screening.
The function returns flagged group keys invisibly and also prints pasteable
R code such as `flagged <- tibble::tibble(country = c("DK", "NO"))`.
This preserves the result even if you did not assign the call to an object.
Use `.print = FALSE` to suppress the console code when desired. Reloading the
browser also ends its session, so restart `screen_timeseries()` to begin again.

**Choose diagnostics inside the app**

All diagnostic tools start switched off. Select any combination of
**Statistics**, **Seasonality**, **Outliers**, **Stationarity**,
**Autocorrelation**, and **Structural breaks** using the checkboxes.
Only selected tools run; results are cached within the session. Your choices
remain active as you navigate through groups. With multiple lines, use
**Series to diagnose** to choose one line for analysis.

Results share a compact panel inside the main graph card. Switch between
enabled analyses using the tabs; each shows its conclusion alongside the
figures or a small diagnostic plot. **Overview** gathers the main findings;
click a finding to open that analysis. Data quality, full outlier tables and
method notes open in dialogs. On desktop screens, the graph adjusts its height
to keep the active results in view. Keys **1** to **6** toggle tools in sidebar
order; arrow keys on a focused result tab switch tabs.

- **Seasonality** adds a dashed trend-plus-season line to the main plot and
  a seasonal profile alongside it. The profile is in the original units.
- **Outliers** marks unusual residual observations on the main plot.
- **Autocorrelation** displays ACF and PACF plots below the main plot.
- **Stationarity** shows KPSS and Phillips--Perron results, including their
  different null hypotheses and interpretations.
- **Structural breaks** marks candidate dates on the main plot and displays
  confidence limits. Choose a level or trend model in the app.

The **Seasonal period** control sets observations per seasonal cycle, such
as 12 for monthly observations with annual seasonality. Leave it blank to
infer annual seasonality for calendar months/quarters; other indices default
to 1 (no seasonality). `.period = 12` can pre-fill this control, but does not
enable any tool. Gaps, duplicate dates and missing/non-finite values are
reported, and prevent time-dependent analysis without silently modifying data.

Descriptive statistics, decomposition, outlier screening and correlations
use base R. Stationarity tests additionally need `feasts` and `urca`;
structural breaks need `strucchange`. The app explains unavailable analyses.
Break searches are limited to 30--2000 observations, use BIC to choose up to
three breaks, and require segments of at least 15% (and at least 10 observations).
Outlier and break markers are candidates for review, not corrections.

The same diagnostic engine is available outside Shiny. Group explicitly by
the columns identifying **one** time series:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df |>
  group_by(country) |>
  diagnose_timeseries(year, gdp, .features = c("summary", "stationarity"))
```

This returns one row per group with scalar statistics and list columns for
test results, outliers, break dates, correlations, decomposition and notes.
See `?diagnose_timeseries` for sample-size requirements and method details.
